soil-formation-s3.title: A farmer describes a dry spring
soil-formation-s3.html:
My grandfather plowed this prairie in the 1920s, when rain was good and wheat paid well. He turned under the grass each fall so the field would be clean for spring. Then came three dry years. With no grass roots to hold it, the top of the field dried to powder, and every strong wind carried it off in brown clouds. Where the topsoil went, the ground underneath was pale and hard, and the wheat that came up there was thin and short. My father spent his life trying to grow back what blew away in a few seasons. I keep the stalks on the field now and leave the hilltops in grass.

Invented passage for practice.

el-nino-la-nina-s3.html:
Over the past three months the trade winds across the central Pacific have been well below normal, and surface water from the date line to the coast of South America is now 1.5 °C warmer than average. Forecasters expect these conditions to last through the coming winter. Coastal Peru and Ecuador should prepare for heavy rain and flooding. Parts of Indonesia and eastern Australia face a higher risk of drought and wildfire. In the United States, the southern states are likely to have a wetter than normal winter. Fishing fleets off Peru should expect smaller catches.

Invented passage for practice, in the style of a seasonal climate outlook.

items.q: What moves Earth's tectonic plates?
options: Convection currents in the hot mantle below the plates
Moving seawater pushing on the edges of the continents
The pull of the Moon on the solid crust each day
Winds blowing across the surface of the ocean plates

items.q: The Himalayas are still rising where the plate carrying India pushes into the plate carrying most of Asia. Which kind of boundary is this?
options: A convergent boundary between two continental plates
A divergent boundary where two plates spread apart
A transform boundary where plates slide side by side
A hot spot under the middle of one plate

items.q: The Hawaiian Islands form a chain. The island of Hawaii in the southeast has active volcanoes, and the islands get older toward the northwest. What best explains this pattern?
options: The Pacific Plate moves northwest over a fixed hot spot
A transform boundary runs along the chain of islands
The islands sit on a divergent boundary that spreads both ways
Each island formed when two ocean plates collided there

items.q: The San Andreas Fault in California causes frequent earthquakes but has few volcanoes. Which kind of plate boundary is it?
options: Transform
Divergent
Convergent, with subduction
Convergent, between two continents

items.q: Many of the world's volcanoes and earthquakes lie in a ring around the Pacific Ocean. Why are they concentrated there?
options: Ocean plates sink under other plates along most of the Pacific edge
The Pacific is the deepest ocean, so the crust there is the thinnest
Hot spots line up in a circle under the middle of the Pacific Plate
Heat moving from warm seawater into the crust melts rock there

items.q: An ocean plate sinks under a continental plate. Which features form at this boundary? Select all that apply.
options: A deep ocean trench
A chain of volcanoes on the continent
A rift valley that splits the continent
A mid-ocean ridge with new seafloor

items.q: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and has many volcanoes. Why does magma reach the surface there?
options: The plates move apart, so pressure drops and hot mantle rock rises and melts
One plate sinks under the other, and the sinking plate melts as it goes down
The plates slide past each other, and friction heats the rock until it melts
The weight of the ocean presses the crust down until it cracks and melts

items.q: Explain why a strong earthquake at a subduction zone under the ocean can cause a tsunami on a distant coast.

cause.label: Cause
options: the sinking plate suddenly slips
the plates slowly drift apart
a hot spot heats the crust

why.1: Slow spreading does not suddenly move the seafloor.
why.2: A hot spot builds volcanoes; it does not lift the seafloor in seconds.

effect.label: What happens
options: the seafloor jumps up and lifts the water above it
the ocean water heats and expands
the trench fills with magma

why.1: Warming water expands far too slowly to make a fast wave.
why.2: Magma does not fill a trench during an earthquake.

result.label: Result
options: sends waves racing across the ocean to the coast
lowers the tide along the coast for a season
stops the plates from moving

why.1: A tsunami arrives in minutes to hours, not over a season.
why.2: An earthquake releases stress; the plates keep moving.

specific.model: When the sinking plate suddenly slips, the seafloor jumps up and lifts the water above it, which causes a series of waves to spread out and rise higher as they reach the shallow water of a distant coast.

items.q: In the diagram, what is happening at the boundary on the left, where the arrows point away from each other?
options: Two plates move apart and magma forms new crust
Two plates collide and one sinks into the mantle
Two plates slide past each other without new crust
A plate moves over a hot spot in the mantle

items.q: According to the diagram, why does the ocean plate, and not the continent, sink at the convergent boundary?
options: Ocean crust is denser than continental crust
Ocean crust is thicker than continental crust
The ocean pushes the plate down with its weight
The continent is moving faster than the ocean plate

items.q: The diagram shows a dashed arrow of magma rising from the sinking plate to a volcano. Which statement explains it?
options: As the plate sinks it heats up, and rock above it melts and rises
The volcano pulls magma up from the mid-ocean ridge on the left
Friction at the transform fault melts rock beneath the continent
Ocean water flows down the trench and boils up through the crust

items.q: A city is built on the continent shown in the diagram, near the trench. Which natural hazards is it most likely to face?
options: Strong earthquakes and volcanic eruptions
Rift valleys opening under the city each year
Hurricanes caused by the sinking plate
Volcanic eruptions but no earthquakes

items.q: What pattern does the graph show?
options: Seafloor rock gets older the farther it is from the ridge
Seafloor rock is about the same age at any distance from the ridge
Seafloor rock gets younger the farther it is from the ridge
Seafloor rock ages quickly near the ridge, then stops aging

items.q: Use the graph. Rock 100 km from the ridge is 4 million years old. What is the average spreading rate on this side of the ridge, in centimeters per year? (1 km = 100,000 cm)

mistakes.why: That is 25 km per million years. Convert: 25 km is 2,500,000 cm, and a million years is 1,000,000 years, so divide 2,500,000 by 1,000,000.
You divided time by distance. A rate is distance divided by time: 10,000,000 cm ÷ 4,000,000 yr.

items.q: The plate moves 2.5 cm each year. How far does it move in 1,000 years? Write the setup with units, then the answer in centimeters.

mistakes.why: Distance is rate times time, not rate divided by time. Multiply: 2.5 cm/yr × 1,000 yr, and the years cancel.
This divides time by the rate, which gives years squared per centimeter. Multiply the rate by the time so the years cancel.
That is 2,500 cm written in meters (25 m). The question asks for centimeters: 2,500 cm.
You divided 1,000 by 2.5. Distance is rate × time: 2.5 × 1,000 = 2,500 cm.

items.q: If the pattern in the graph continues, how old is seafloor rock 150 km from the ridge?
options: 6 million years
3 million years
4 million years
150 million years

items.q: Which two processes form soil?
options: Weathering of parent material and the decay of organic matter
Erosion of topsoil and the deposit of salt by floodwater
Photosynthesis in roots and evaporation from the soil surface
Compaction by heavy machines and the melting of bedrock

items.q: Soil in a tropical rainforest forms faster than soil in the tundra on the same kind of rock. What best explains this?
options: Warmth and water speed up weathering and decomposition
Rainforest bedrock is softer than tundra bedrock everywhere
Tundra plants add more organic matter, which slows soil formation
Wind erosion is stronger in the rainforest, which adds new soil

items.q: What is humus?
options: Dark, decomposed organic matter in soil
The solid rock layer under the soil
Clay that has washed down into the subsoil
Water stored in the spaces between soil grains

items.q: Why does wind remove more soil from a field after it is plowed than from the same field covered in grass?
options: Plowed soil is loose and bare, with no roots to hold it
Plowing adds organic matter that is light enough for the wind to lift
Grass makes the wind blow faster over a field than over bare soil
Plowing moves the C horizon to the surface, which is lighter than topsoil

items.q: A forest on a steep hillside is cut down and the land is left bare. Explain how this can harm a river at the bottom of the hill.

cause.label: First link
options: removes the roots that hold soil in place
adds humus to the topsoil
raises the water table under the hill

why.1: Cutting trees reduces the leaves and wood that become humus.
why.2: The question is about soil washing downhill, not the water table.

effect.label: Next link
options: rain washes more soil downhill into the river
the soil forms faster on the bare slope
the river carries less sediment than before

why.1: Bare soil erodes; it does not form faster.
why.2: With more erosion, the river carries more sediment, not less.

result.label: Harm to the river
options: makes the water cloudy and buries the gravel where fish lay eggs
cools the water so fish grow faster
removes nutrients from the river water

why.1: Less shade warms a stream; and fish growing faster would not be harm.
why.2: Eroded soil carries nutrients into the river; it does not remove them.

specific.model: Removing the trees removes the roots that hold soil in place, so rain washes more soil downhill into the river, which causes the water to turn cloudy with sediment, blocks sunlight and buries the gravel where fish lay their eggs.

items.q: In the soil profile, which horizon is topsoil, with the most humus mixed into the minerals and most of the roots?
options: The A horizon

The O horizon

items.q: The diagram says minerals leached from above collect in the B horizon. What carries them down?

Roots pulling minerals down from the surface
Wind blowing minerals into cracks in the soil
Heat rising from the bedrock below the soil

items.q: Why does the C horizon in the diagram contain chunks of rock but very little humus?
options: It is near the bedrock, far below the fallen leaves
Humus is heavier than rock, so it sinks below the C horizon
Decomposers in the C horizon turn rock fragments into humus

items.q: The diagram notes that soil forms slowly, often taking centuries for a few centimeters. What does this mean for a farm that loses 1 cm of topsoil to erosion every year?
options: Soil is lost far faster than it forms, so the topsoil thins
It is losing soil at the same rate it forms, so the topsoil stays the same
New soil forms faster after erosion, so the loss will be replaced in a year
The loss does not matter, because crops grow mostly in the C horizon

items.q: What pattern does the table show?
options: Less ground cover goes with more soil lost
Plowing the soil reduces the amount of soil lost
Each plot loses roughly the same amount of soil each year
Leaving stalks on the ground increases soil loss

items.q: A farmer switches a field from bare, plowed soil with a crop (plot 3) to keeping the leftover stalks on the ground (plot 2). Write the setup for the percent change in soil lost, then the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the old value, 12.0, the soil lost before the change, not by the new value.
Subtract old from new: (new - old). Here the loss went down, so the percent change is negative.
Put the difference in brackets. Without them the division happens first: (2.5 - 12.0) / 12.0 × 100.
You left out the × 100. A fraction of −0.79 is a change of about −79%.
That is the change from 2.5 up to 12.0. The farmer moved from 12.0 to 2.5, so start from 12.0.

items.q: Plot 4 loses 30.0 metric tons of soil per hectare per year. How much soil does a 40-hectare field like plot 4 lose in one year, in metric tons?

mistakes.why: You divided 30.0 by 40. Each hectare loses 30.0 metric tons, so multiply by the 40 hectares.
You added. The loss is 30.0 metric tons for each of 40 hectares: 30.0 × 40.

items.q: Which conclusion do the data support?
options: More plant cover goes with less soil loss on this slope
Growing a crop doubles soil loss compared with leaving soil bare
Plowing makes little difference to soil loss on this slope

items.q: What is the main claim of the passage?
options: Plowing up the grass let drought winds strip the topsoil away
Wheat grows better in prairie soil that is plowed each fall
Drought by itself, not the way the land was farmed, caused the loss

items.q: Which detail in the passage best supports the claim that losing topsoil hurt the farm?
options: "the wheat that came up there was thin and short"
"when rain was good and wheat paid well"
"He turned under the grass each fall so the field would be clean"

items.q: The farmer says, "My father spent his life trying to grow back what blew away in a few seasons." What does this sentence assume about soil?
options: Topsoil forms far more slowly than it can be lost
Topsoil can be rebuilt in a few years by planting more seed
Subsoil grows crops as well as topsoil does

items.q: Which list puts soil particles in order from largest to smallest?
options: Sand, silt, clay
Clay, silt, sand
Silt, sand, clay
Sand, clay, silt

items.q: Why does water drain through a sandy soil faster than through a clay soil?
options: Sand has large, connected pores that water flows through
Sand holds more humus, which pulls water down through the soil
Clay grains are larger, so they block the water from passing
Clay particles pack so tightly that clay has almost no pores

items.q: A gardener wants a soil that holds enough water for plants but still drains so roots get air. Which soil texture fits best?
options: Loam
Sand
Clay
Silty clay

items.q: Why is a soil rich in clay and humus usually more fertile than a sandy soil?
options: Clay and humus hold nutrients against leaching
Clay and humus let water pass through faster than sand
Sand grains release substances that are toxic to roots

items.q: A soil test shows a field's soil has a pH of 4.5. What does this tell the farmer?
options: It is strongly acidic, which limits nutrients for many crops
It is close to neutral, which suits most crops very well
It is basic, so it will hold far too much water for crops
It is high in humus, so it needs little or no fertilizer

items.q: A soil sample is 35% sand and 45% silt. The rest is clay. What percent of the sample is clay?

mistakes.why: That is the sand and silt together (35 + 45). Clay is what is left: 100 - 80.
Subtract the sum of sand and silt from 100: 100 - (35 + 45) = 20.

items.q: On the triangle, which sample is a loam?
options: Sample B
Sample A
Sample C
Sample D

items.q: Sample D is 6% clay and 20% sand. What percent of sample D is silt?

mistakes.why: That is the clay and sand together. Silt is the rest: 100 - 26 = 74%.
You subtracted 6 from 20. The three parts add to 100%: 100 - (6 + 20) = 74%.

items.q: Which sample would hold the most water but let water pass through it most slowly?
options: Sample C
Sample A
Sample B

items.q: A town wants to build a sewage drain field, where wastewater soaks slowly into the soil, which needs soil that drains steadily. Which sample would cause the most trouble, and why?
options: Sample C: its tiny pores drain so slowly that water pools
Sample B: loam drains much too fast to filter the water
Sample A: sand holds water so tightly it barely drains
Sample D: silt has too little pore space for water to move

items.q: Which statement describes the data in the table?
options: Soils that drained more slowly held more water
Sand held the most water and also drained the most slowly
The three soils held roughly equal amounts of water
Clay drained the most water out of its column

items.q: The water in the loam column traveled 10 cm in 10 minutes. Find the percolation rate in centimeters per hour. Write the setup with units, then the answer. (1 hour = 60 minutes)

mistakes.why: Dividing by 60 again leaves min² on the bottom. Multiply by 60 min per hour so the minutes cancel.
A rate is distance over time; this puts time on top.
That is 1 cm per minute. The question asks per hour: multiply by 60.
You divided by 60. There are 60 minutes in an hour, so the water moves 60 times farther in an hour.

items.q: What percent of the 200 mL poured on the clay column did the clay hold?

mistakes.why: You left out the × 100. 110 ÷ 200 is 0.55, which is 55%.
That is the share that drained out (90 of 200). The clay held 110 of 200 mL.

items.q: Why did the class use the same depth of soil and the same 200 mL of water for every soil?
options: So any difference in drainage comes from the soil type
So that each soil would end up holding the same water
So that the sand would drain as slowly as the clay did
So the class could skip timing the water in each column

items.q: Write a testable hypothesis for this experiment about clay content and drainage time.

change.label: If
options: the clay content of the soil increases
more water is poured on the soil
the room is warmer

why.1: The volume of water was held constant at 200 mL.
why.2: Room temperature is not what the class changed.

variable.label: Then
options: the time for water to pass through the column
the depth of the soil column
the color of the soil

why.1: Depth was held constant at 10 cm.
why.2: The class measured time and volume, not color.

direction.label: Will
options: increase
be affected
change

why.1: "Be affected" does not say which way; a hypothesis gives a direction.
why.2: "Change" does not say which way; say increase or decrease.

specific.model: If the clay content of the soil increases, then the time for 200 mL of water to drain through a 10 cm column will increase.

items.q: In which layer of the atmosphere does almost all weather happen?
options: Troposphere
Stratosphere
Mesosphere
Thermosphere

items.q: What does the ozone layer do for life on Earth's surface?
options: Absorbs most harmful ultraviolet light
Traps heat near the ground to warm Earth
Supplies the oxygen that animals breathe
Reflects sunlight to keep the surface cool

items.q: Why does the temperature rise with height in the stratosphere?
options: Ozone there absorbs ultraviolet light
It is closer to the Sun than the troposphere
Warm air from the ground rises and collects there
Clouds in the stratosphere trap heat from below

items.q: Why does air get colder as you climb a mountain?
options: The air is heated from the ground, and rising air cools
Air higher up sits closer to the cold ozone layer
Mountains block sunlight from reaching their peaks
Air higher up holds more oxygen, which absorbs heat

items.q: A town at sea level is 20 °C. Air in the troposphere cools about 6.5 °C for every kilometer you rise. What is the temperature on a peak 3 km above the town?

mistakes.why: You added. Temperature falls with height in the troposphere: 20 - (6.5 × 3).
That is the drop for 1 km. For 3 km the drop is 6.5 × 3 = 19.5 °C.
19.5 °C is the drop, not the temperature. Subtract it from 20 °C.

items.q: Ozone near the ground irritates the lungs, but ozone high in the stratosphere protects life. How can the same gas be harmful in one place and helpful in another?
options: High up it blocks UV light; near the ground people breathe it in
Ozone in the stratosphere is a different chemical from ground ozone
Ozone is harmless at any height; near the ground it carries soil dust
Ozone near the ground absorbs more UV light, which burns the lungs

items.q: Which statements about the atmosphere are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Nitrogen is the most common gas in dry air
The ozone layer is in the troposphere
Most of the air's mass is in the thermosphere
Oxygen makes up about half of dry air

items.q: According to the graph, how does temperature change from the ground up to about 11 km?
options: It falls steadily, from 15 °C to −56.5 °C
It rises steadily, from 15 °C to −56.5 °C
It stays the same at about 15 °C
It falls, then rises, then falls again

items.q: Use the graph. From 0 km to 11 km the temperature goes from 15 °C to −56.5 °C. What is the average change in temperature per kilometer?

mistakes.why: Subtract the starting temperature: −56.5 − 15 = −71.5, not −56.5 + 15.
That is the total change. Divide by the 11 km to get the change per kilometer.
The temperature falls, so the change per kilometer is negative: −6.5 °C/km.

items.q: The graph shows temperature rising from about 20 km to 47 km. Which layer is this, and what causes the warming?
options: The stratosphere, where ozone absorbs UV light
The troposphere, where the ground heats the air
The mesosphere, where the air is heated by meteors
The thermosphere, where clouds trap heat

items.q: A plane cruises at 11 km, near the top of the troposphere. Which part of the graph explains why storms rarely rise much above that height?
options: Above 11 km temperature stops falling, so rising air is no longer warmer than its surroundings
Above 11 km temperature drops much faster, so the clouds freeze solid and fall back down
The graph shows the air is at its warmest at 11 km, so storms stop growing at that height
The graph shows too little air above 11 km for clouds to form in

items.q: According to the table, about what fraction of dry air is oxygen?
options: About one fifth
About one half
About three quarters
About one tenth

items.q: Use the table. In a sample of 1,000,000 molecules of dry air, about how many are argon?
Use the table. Carbon dioxide is 0.042% of dry air by volume. Scientists usually give it in parts per million (ppm): molecules per 1,000,000 molecules of air. What is 0.042% in ppm?

mistakes.why: Too small by a factor of 10. 1% is 10,000 ppm, so 0.042% is 0.042 × 10,000 = 420 ppm.
Too large by a factor of 10. 0.042 ÷ 100 × 1,000,000 = 420 ppm.

items.q: A student says, "Carbon dioxide is such a tiny part of the air that changes in it cannot matter." Which response uses the table and the course correctly?
options: A small share can matter: plants need CO2, and it helps hold heat near the surface
The student is right, because nitrogen and oxygen are what affect living things
The student is right, because argon is a larger share and it does not matter
The table is wrong, because carbon dioxide is really about 21% of the air

items.q: What sets global winds in motion in the first place?
options: The Sun heats the equator more than the poles
The Moon's gravity pulls the air toward the equator
Mountains push air up wherever they stand
Ocean waves drag the air along with them

items.q: Why do the trade winds in the Northern Hemisphere blow from the northeast instead of straight from the north?
options: Earth's rotation turns moving air to the right

Mountains along the equator turn the wind to the west

items.q: Which way does the Coriolis effect deflect moving air in the Southern Hemisphere?
options: To the left of its direction of motion
To the right of its direction of motion
Straight up, away from the ground

items.q: Many of the world's large deserts, such as the Sahara, lie near 30° N or 30° S. Why?
options: Dry air sinks there and warms, so clouds rarely form
The trade winds blow sand from the equator to 30°

items.q: Tropical rainforests are found near the equator. How do global wind patterns help explain this?
options: Warm, moist air rises there and cools into rain
Cold air sinks at the equator and brings steady rain
The westerlies carry rain from the poles to the equator
Air at the equator stays still, so rain falls straight down

items.q: Put the steps of the Hadley cell in order, starting at the equator.
options: Air is heated at the equator and rises
Rising air cools and drops rain
Dry air spreads toward the poles high up
Air sinks near 30° and warms
Air flows back toward the equator along the surface as the trade winds

items.q: In the diagram, which winds blow at the surface between about 30° N and 60° N?
options: The westerlies
The northeast trade winds
The polar easterlies
The southeast trade winds

items.q: The diagram shows air rising at both the equator and 60°, and sinking at 30° and the poles. Which statement explains the pattern of wet and dry places it labels?
options: Rising air cools and makes rain; sinking air warms and dries
Sinking air cools and makes rain; rising air warms and dries
Places with rising air get less sunlight, so they stay wet
Sinking air carries water down from the upper air as rain

items.q: A sailing ship leaves Spain (about 40° N) and heads for the Caribbean (about 15° N). According to the diagram, which winds should it use for the long crossing west?
options: The northeast trade winds, after sailing south to below 30° N

The trade winds carry air from west to east at these latitudes

items.q: Which latitude band in the graph gets the most precipitation?
Use the graph. How many times more precipitation falls in the 0-10° N band than in the 20-30° N band? Give your answer to one decimal place.

mistakes.why: You divided the smaller value by the larger. "How many times more" puts the larger value on top: 2,000 ÷ 450.
That is how many more millimeters, not how many times more. Divide: 2,000 ÷ 450.

items.q: Which pattern of air motion matches the shape of the graph?
options: Rising air near 0° and 60°, sinking air near 30°
Sinking air near 0° and 60°, rising air near 30°

items.q: A student concludes from the graph that places farther from the equator always get less rain. Is this conclusion supported?
options: No: the 40-60° N band gets more rain than the 20-30° N band
Yes: each band is drier than the band closer to the equator
Yes: the 60-80° N band is the driest band on the graph
No: the 0-10° N band gets less rain than the 10-20° N band

items.q: Explain why the area near 30° N is dry, starting from the heating at the equator.

specific.frame: Air heated at the equator ___, then ___, so near 30° N ___.

first.label: At the equator
options: rises, cools and drops its rain
sinks and warms
stays still and absorbs water

why.1: Heated air is light, so it rises; it does not sink at the equator.
why.2: Heated air rises; it does not stay still.

then.label: Next
options: the dry air moves toward the poles high up
the moist air flows north along the ground
the air freezes into ice in the upper air

why.1: At the surface near 30° the trade winds flow toward the equator, not away from it.
why.2: The air does not freeze into ice; it moves poleward.

result.label: Near 30° N
options: the air sinks and warms, so clouds rarely form
the air rises and makes heavy rain
the air cools and makes snow

why.1: Air sinks near 30°; rising air near 30° would make rain.
why.2: Sinking air warms; it does not cool.

specific.model: Air heated at the equator rises, cools and drops its rain, then the dry air moves toward the poles high up, so near 30° N it sinks and warms, which causes clouds to evaporate and leaves the land dry.

items.q: What is a watershed?
options: The land that drains into one stream, river or lake
A layer of rock and sediment that stores groundwater
A dam built to hold water for a city
The point where a river reaches the ocean

items.q: What separates one watershed from the next?
options: A divide: a ridge or high ground
A river: the main channel in the valley
A dam: a wall across the valley
A water table: the top of the groundwater

items.q: A town takes its drinking water from a river. A factory 80 km upstream, in the same watershed, starts dumping waste into a small stream that feeds the river. Why should the town be concerned?
options: Streams in a watershed flow down to the same river
The waste will soak into the aquifer under the factory
Waste in a small stream evaporates before reaching a river
Streams flow toward their sources, so waste stays upstream

items.q: Two watersheds get the same storm. One is mostly forest and the other is mostly pavement and rooftops. Which statement best describes the difference?
options: The paved one has more runoff and higher floods

Both have equal runoff, because they got the same rain
The paved one has more infiltration into groundwater

items.q: Which features of a watershed increase the runoff and erosion that follow a storm? Select all that apply.

Deep, sandy soil
Thick forest cover

items.q: A news report says a city "draws its water from the Ogallala Aquifer, in the Platte River watershed." What is the difference between the two terms?
options: A watershed is land draining to a river; an aquifer stores water underground
An aquifer is land draining to a river; a watershed stores water underground

items.q: In the map view, rain falls just outside the dashed divide of watershed A, on the side toward watershed B. Where does that water go?

items.q: Propose a way to reduce sediment entering a stream from a steep, plowed field next to it, and say how it works.

specific.frame: Plant ___ along the stream, which ___, so ___.

action.label: Action
options: a strip of grass and trees
a row of fertilized crops
nothing, leaving the bank bare

why.1: More plowed, fertilized crops leave soil exposed and add nutrients to runoff.
why.2: Bare banks erode easily.

how.label: How it works
options: slows runoff and lets roots hold the soil
speeds runoff into the stream
raises the water temperature

why.1: Speeding runoff increases erosion.
why.2: Warmer water does not stop sediment.

result.label: Result
options: less sediment reaches the stream
more sediment reaches the stream
the watershed gets larger

why.1: The goal is to reduce sediment.
why.2: Plants do not change the area of the watershed.

specific.model: Plant a strip of grass and trees along the stream, which slows runoff so sediment settles out, and the roots hold the bank soil, which reduces the sediment that reaches the stream.

items.q: Mill Creek flows into the Ohio River, which flows into the Mississippi River. How is the Mill Creek watershed related to the Mississippi River watershed?
options: It is a small part of the Mississippi watershed

items.q: Explain why a city at 45° N has longer days in June than in December.

cause.label: Cause
options: North Pole is tilted toward the Sun
Earth is closest to the Sun
Sun gives off more light

why.1: Earth is closest to the Sun in January, not June.
why.2: The Sun's output hardly changes over the year.

effect.label: Effect
options: the Sun stays above the horizon longer each day
Earth spins more slowly
the city moves closer to the equator

why.1: Earth spins at the same rate all year.
why.2: The city stays at 45° N.

result.label: Result
options: gives the city more hours of daylight
gives the city fewer hours of daylight
keeps the hours of daylight the same

why.1: Longer time above the horizon means more daylight, not less.
why.2: Day length does change with the seasons at 45° N.

specific.model: In June the North Pole is tilted toward the Sun, so the Sun stays above the horizon longer each day, which means the city gets more hours of daylight than in December, when the tilt points it away.

items.q: On about March 20 and September 22, day and night are each about 12 hours long almost everywhere on Earth. What is true of Earth's tilt on those dates?

Earth's axis stops being tilted for a day

items.q: What is a rain shadow?

A wet area at the foot of the slope that faces the wind
The shade that a large storm cloud casts on the ground
A cold, snowy area high up on a mountain peak

The trees on the slope absorb water vapor directly from the air
Rising air is squeezed, so the water is pushed out of it

items.q: Explain why the east side of a north-south mountain range in the westerlies (30° to 60° N) is often dry.

what.label: What the wind carries
options: moist air up the west slope
dry air up the east slope
cold air down from the pole

why.1: The westerlies blow from the west, so air climbs the west slope first.
why.2: The westerlies blow from the west, not from the pole.

how.label: How it changes
options: cools and drops its rain on the west side
warms and gains water on the west side
stays the same over the mountains

why.1: Rising air cools and loses water; it does not gain it.
why.2: Air crossing a range rises and cools, then sinks and warms.

result.label: Result on the east side

the east side gets the heaviest rain
the east side is covered by glaciers

why.1: The heaviest rain falls on the windward (west) side.
why.2: The east side is dry, not icy.

specific.model: The westerlies carry moist air up the west slope, which cools as it rises and drops its rain there, so the air sinking down the east side is dry and warms, which leads to a rain shadow.
